title: Job 42:7–9
context: The narrator reports that after speaking to Job, the LORD addresses Eliphaz the Temanite: “My wrath is kindled against you, and against your two friends; for you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.” The LORD tells the three to offer seven bulls and seven rams and to go to Job, who will pray for them, and the narrator reports that Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar obey and that “the LORD accepted Job.” What Job said that was right is debated, and the verdict names Eliphaz and his two friends without mentioning Elihu, about which the text says nothing further; both traditions share the ground that Job’s intercession and the LORD’s acceptance are gifts of grace.

verses.text: It was so, that after the LORD had spoken these words to Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “My wrath is kindled against you, and against your two friends; for you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Eliphaz, “you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.” Arminian readers note that the options discussed include Job’s honest speech to God, his refusal of the friends’ scheme, and his final submission.

The text does not specify which.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise weigh these options and do not claim certainty, and may note that the LORD commends Job without endorsing every word he spoke (cf. 42:3).

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the LORD rejects the friends’ account of Job’s suffering, and that the verdict names Eliphaz and his two friends.

verses.text: Now therefore, take to yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and offer up for yourselves a burnt offering; and my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept him, that I not deal with you according to your folly. For you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept him.” Arminian readers note that the one the friends accused becomes the one who intercedes for them.

Job had offered burnt offerings for his children in 1:5; now he prays for those who wounded him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God appointing a mediator and accepting the offering and the prayer, and some see a pattern that points ahead to Christ, held as a hedged reading.

Shared ground: both traditions see the intercession theme here (cf. Gen 20:7; Jas 5:16) and note that the LORD repeats that the friends “have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.”

verses.text: So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went and did what the LORD commanded them, and the LORD accepted Job.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went and did what the LORD commanded them, and the LORD accepted Job.” Arminian readers note the friends’ obedience.

They are not cast off but restored through Job’s prayer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see grace extended to the friends through the means God appointed.

Shared ground: both traditions note that the three friends named in 2:11 are named again here, and that the LORD’s acceptance of Job is the closing word of the scene.
